entities.summary:
The Party for Freedom (Partij voor de Vrijheid), founded on February 22, 2006, in Amsterdam, Netherlands, stands as a significant political entity within the contemporary European landscape. Established by Geert Wilders, the party emerged in response to growing concerns over immigration, national identity, and political correctness in the Netherlands and across Western Europe. With a platform that advocates for a stricter immigration policy and a reduction of the influence of Islam in Dutch society, the party has garnered considerable attention and controversy, reflecting broader debates around nationalism and multiculturalism in Europe.

In the years following its inception, the Party for Freedom quickly rose in prominence, becoming the third-largest party in the Dutch parliament by the 2010 elections, claiming 24 of the 150 seats. Wilders' inflammatory rhetoric and the party's critical stance towards the European Union resonated with a significant portion of the electorate, particularly amidst the backdrop of economic crises and increasing public discontent with traditional parties. The party has been involved in various coalitions and has influenced national debates on integration, security, and civil liberties, marking its presence on both the national and European stages.

The legacy of the Party for Freedom is evident in the subsequent rise of other populist and right-wing parties across Europe, as it has inspired similar movements in countries such as France and Germany. Its focus on anti-immigration and national sovereignty themes has transformed the political discourse, compelling mainstream parties to adopt more hardline stances on immigration and integration policies. This shift reflects a broader trend of nationalism and populism that has shaped electoral outcomes and policy decisions in multiple European nations.
